You're designing a part for someone to 3D print at home. They'll print it on their own printer, use only the hardware listed below, and put it together by following your manual.

## Their setup
- Printer: Bambu Lab X1C (with AMS), build volume 256 x 256 x 256 mm
- Nozzle: 0.4 mm
- Layer height: 0.2 mm
- Filament: PLA (high-speed PLA, black)
- Longest bridge seen to print cleanly on this setup: 50 mm
- Supports: none. Every part has to print without them.

## Hardware they can use
Refer to an item by its catalog reference: "ISO 4762 M5x30" (socket head screw, size x length, from the lengths listed), "ISO 4032 M5" (hex nut), "ISO 10511 M5" (nylon-insert lock nut), "ISO 7089 M5" (washer), "ASME B18.2.2 1/4-20" (1/4"-20 nut), "insert M3x4x5" (heat-set insert), "salvaged:webcam-mount-bolt".

## How to work
You have these tools:
- measure(item, what): ask the person to measure one of their own things, such as their desk or their phone. They answer with what they measured, or say they can't measure it.
- print_test(params, parts): optional. If you need to know whether something is going to work but you're not sure, ask the person to print a test of it before you hand in the final design, so you both save time and filament. They print it and tell you how each piece came out.
- submit_design(...): hand in the finished design. This ends the conversation.
- report_limitation(wanted, blocked_by, why): say you wanted to use something (a technique, a tool, a part or material, a way of handing in the design) but couldn't because of what's available here. It doesn't change anything, but it's noted.
You have at most 12 turns. Hand in a design before they run out.

## The design you hand in
submit_design's schema describes every field. The rules that matter:
- Every dimension that comes from hardware or the real world is a named param, with its source: measured (the person measured it for you), datasheet, catalog, asked (the person told you), guessed, unknown, or design (your own choice).
- Each part's `code` is Python that defines build(p) and returns a CadQuery Workplane or Shape. `cq` is already imported, and p.<name> is each param's value. Dimensions that come from hardware or the real world must come from params.
- Model each part in the orientation it's printed in, with z = 0 on the bed.
- The manual is the steps the person follows, naming the parts and hardware each step uses.

I borrowed my friend's tripod, and I can't seem to find the part that connects the camera to the tripod. How hard would it be to 3D print it, both the flat part and the part that screws in? Just as a temporary thing until I find the real one. I know it's metal normally.

The real constraint is that the plate has to fit the tripod's quick-release clamp, so I need the clamp's opening dimensions, and I'm checking whether it uses the Arca-Swiss standard

content: tripod clamp style: jaws with angled lips, tightened by a knob; the plate drops in from above; tripod clamp plate width: 38 mm (the width of plate it takes)
webcam bolt head across: about 15 mm (its head); webcam bolt head height: about 5 mm (its head); webcam bolt length: about 10 mm (under the head)

reasoning:
I'm working out the Arca-Swiss plate specs: 38 mm width with a 45° dovetail, roughly 10 mm total thickness, and a 10 mm bolt under the head. The camera socket is only about 5–6 mm deep, so the plate's base thickness around the bolt has to stay near 5 mm or less for the bolt to project into it.

I'm checking the plate geometry against the camera socket: a 10 mm bolt head in a 5 mm counterbore leaves about 5 mm of bolt projecting, which is at the limit of the socket depth. I'm also thinking about printing the dovetail profile as a small test coupon to check the fit in the clamp before printing the full plate.

I'm sketching the Arca profile in more detail now: a flat 38 mm top, a short 2 mm vertical edge, then a 45° bevel down to about 30 mm wide, with the body narrowing below that so the clamp jaws only catch the bevel. I'm also checking that the plate stays around 9–10 mm thick overall, which is typical.

I'm weighing whether the salvaged bolt is the better choice over a printed 1/4-20 thread in PLA, and I'm wondering how to make the head reachable for tightening. A recessed counterbore would hide the thumbwheel, so I'm considering a finger slot across it or simply rotating the camera onto the bolt instead.

I'm weighing a slot or channel in the plate so I can reach the bolt head, since a fully recessed 15 mm head is otherwise impossible to turn. Cutting across the whole width would weaken the plate, and widening the counterbore leaves too little material at the narrower bottom, so I'm leaning toward a finger slot along the length instead.

I'm picturing the full-length slot now: about 16.5 mm wide and 5 mm deep along the underside, so the bolt head sits in it and its edge is reachable from both ends. I'm checking whether the walls left beside it are thick enough once the bottom narrows to 30 mm.

Next I'm weighing a simple coupon print to test the dovetail fit before committing to the full plate. The bolt hole will be about 6.8 mm for the 1/4" clearance, with a 16.5 mm counterbore above it.

Still writing the plate profile code...

Checking the bolt projection again: a 10 mm plate with a 5 mm counterbore leaves a 5 mm bolt sticking out, which should fit the camera socket. I'll run a short test coupon with the hole and pocket to confirm the clamp fit before committing to the full plate.
